1.11 Writing a plugin

A plugin is a Rust crate that implements the Plugin trait from diskproxy-core and is linked into the application at build time. There is no dynamic loading: adding a plugin means adding a crate and registering it in src/main.rs. The plugin guide gives every step, and the hide example is a complete, compiled reference with a patch that registers it.

1.11.1 The trait

pub trait Plugin: Send + Sync {
    fn identity(&self) -> Option<String> { None }
    fn visible(&self, _parts: &[String], _metadata: &Metadata) -> Result<bool> { Ok(true) }
    fn mtime(&self, _parts: &[String], metadata: &Metadata) -> Result<i64> { Ok(metadata.mtime()) }
    fn compose(&self, _parts: &[String], _file: &File) -> Result<Option<Vec<Piece>>> { Ok(None) }
    fn written(&self, _parts: &[String], _file: &File) -> Result<()> { Ok(()) }
}

Every method has a default, so a plugin overrides only what it needs. parts are the path components relative to the source root.

Hook Return Meaning
identity Stable string or None Seeds the disk’s volume serial; None derives it from the source
visible true or false Shows or hides an entry, on direct opens as well as in listings
mtime Unix seconds The modification time to present; the source keeps its own
compose Pieces or None Presents a file as a sequence of pieces; None serves it unchanged
written () A client wrote this file on a writable view; file holds its new bytes

An error aborts the operation; it is never a request to fall back to the unmodified entry. Keep the hooks deterministic for a session, because the disk is built from one snapshot of the tree. Plugins are shared across threads.

1.11.2 Composing files

pub enum Piece {
    Bytes(Vec<u8>),
    Own { offset: u64, length: u64 },
    Other {
        source: Arc<Source>,
        path: Arc<str>,
        offset: u64,
        length: u64,
        stamp: Option<Stamp>,
    },
}

Bytes are generated by the plugin, Own is a range of the file being presented, and Other is a range of a file under another root. Open that root with Source::new, so it gets the same read-only, no-symlink rules. The core checks every range against the file’s size, records each file’s size and modification time, and refuses reads once either changes. When the plugin already knows another file’s size and modification time, it can pass them as stamp, so the scan doesn’t open that file; the stamp is still checked on every read. Composed files are served identically by all three transports.

1.11.3 Receiving writes

written is called with a read-only handle to the new bytes: from the NFS overlay, or from the mounted volume for a harvested shadow-file view. The source is never written, and the handle cannot write to it. A plugin that saves something should save it outside the source, as the previews plugin’s ratings folder must be, and should treat the call as untrusted input: temporary files, partial saves and files the application writes for its own purposes all arrive here.

1.11.4 Registering and testing

To register a plugin, add its crate to the workspace and the application’s dependencies, add its name to PluginName in src/main.rs, validate its plugins.<name> settings before any setup I/O, and add a construction arm that returns the source, the plugin and its startup information. Test with synthetic folders only, through both direct opens and listings, and confirm that the source files are unchanged afterwards.

A plugin is trusted code. The trait is a policy boundary, not a sandbox: a plugin can call any API Rust allows, so keep its own writes small, explicit and documented.
